The n side of an abrupt junction is ten times more lightly doped than the p side. Where does the depletion region extend farther?
choices: Into the n side, about ten times farther
Into the p side, about ten times farther
questions.explain: Charge balance requires N_A x_p = N_D x_n, so the less doped n side takes more width.

questions.stem: What happens to the junction barrier and depletion width when a PN diode is forward biased?
questions.explain: The applied forward voltage opposes the built-in barrier and narrows depletion.

questions.stem: What does increasing the reverse bias of an abrupt PN junction do before breakdown?
choices: It widens depletion and raises the peak electric field
It narrows depletion and raises the peak field
It widens depletion and lowers the peak field
questions.explain: Higher reverse voltage increases both depletion width and peak field for fixed doping.

questions.stem: An unbiased PN junction has a nonzero built-in electric field. Why is its net current zero?
choices: No carriers can move across the junction
Electrons and holes have identical mobility
The electric field is canceled everywhere
questions.explain: The opposing drift and diffusion currents cancel at equilibrium.

questions.stem: At fixed temperature, N_A is multiplied by 10 while N_D is unchanged. How does V_bi change?
questions.explain: The dopant product inside the logarithm increases by a factor of ten.

questions.stem: An abrupt junction has V_bi = 0.7 V and a reverse bias of 2.3 V. What voltage magnitude appears across the depletion region?
questions.explain: In reverse bias the depletion region supports V_bi + V_R.

questions.stem: Two varactors have the same doping and reverse bias. One has twice the junction area. How do their capacitances compare?
choices: The larger one has twice the capacitance
The larger one has half the capacitance
The larger one has four times the capacitance
questions.explain: With the same depletion width, C_j = ε_s A / W scales with area.

questions.stem: A measured capacitance drops from 12 pF to 6 pF as reverse bias increases. What happened to depletion width at fixed area?
choices: It increased by a factor of four
questions.explain: Junction capacitance is inversely proportional to depletion width.

questions.stem: Which plot is expected to be approximately linear for an abrupt PN junction before breakdown?
questions.explain: C_j is proportional to (V_bi + V_R) raised to −1/2 for an abrupt junction.

questions.stem: An abrupt junction has W = 0.50 μm. Total depletion voltage increases by a factor of nine. What is the new W?
questions.explain: The width grows by the square root of nine.

questions.stem: A forward-biased diode current doubles at fixed temperature and ideality factor. What happens to its small-signal resistance?
questions.explain: The incremental resistance is approximately n V_T / I_D.

questions.stem: Two diodes follow the exponential approximation at the same temperature. For the same voltage increase, which has the larger current multiplication factor?
choices: The answer depends only on area
questions.explain: The exponent increment is ΔV/(n V_T), which is larger for n = 1.

questions.stem: At 300 K, a diode with n = 1 carries 2 mA. Using V_T = 26 mV, what is its small-signal resistance?
questions.explain: Divide 26 mV by 2 mA to get 13 Ω.

questions.stem: In the ideal diode law, I_S = 3 nA. What current is expected well into reverse bias, before breakdown?
choices: A large negative current that grows exponentially with reverse bias
questions.explain: In reverse bias, the exponential term tends to zero, leaving −I_S.

questions.stem: In the charge-control model, a forward-biased diode has Q = 30 nC at I_D = 10 mA. What is the carrier lifetime estimate?
questions.explain: Use τ ≈ Q/I_D = 30 nC / 10 mA.

questions.stem: A silicon PN diode switches from a larger forward current, with lifetime and reverse removal current unchanged. How does the storage interval change?
questions.explain: Larger forward current stores more minority charge, which takes longer to remove.

questions.stem: Two identical PN diodes start with the same forward current. The second driver provides more reverse removal current. Which diode stops conducting reverse recovery current sooner?
questions.explain: Greater reverse removal current clears the same initial stored charge faster.

questions.stem: Which mechanism dominates the reverse breakdown of a heavily doped junction with a very thin depletion region?
choices: Thermal motion with no electric field
questions.explain: A narrow, high-field depletion layer allows Zener tunneling.

questions.stem: In avalanche breakdown, why can reverse current rise sharply?
choices: Accelerated carriers generate new electron–hole pairs by collisions
The applied voltage removes all ionized dopants
questions.explain: Impact ionization generates mobile carriers that can create further pairs.

questions.stem: An idealized triangular field profile has the same peak field but twice the depletion width. What happens to the voltage represented by its area?
questions.explain: The field integral is E_max W / 2 for a triangular profile.

questions.stem: A long diode has the same minority-carrier diffusion coefficient but one quarter of the lifetime. How does diffusion length change?
questions.explain: The diffusion length is √(Dτ).

questions.stem: Under strong forward bias at fixed temperature, why does diffusion capacitance rise as the diode current rises?
choices: More minority charge is stored and changes more strongly with voltage
The depletion region widens far into both neutral regions
questions.explain: Forward injection stores minority carriers, and diffusion capacitance measures the change in stored charge with voltage.

pages.title: pn junction built-in potential
body: At equilibrium, electrons and holes diffuse across the junction until drift balances diffusion.
V_bi = V_T ln(N_A N_D / n_i^2), where V_T ≈ 0.026 V at 300 K.

pages.title: Depletion width and charge
body: Forward bias narrows depletion. Reverse bias widens it and raises the peak field.
Depletion extends farther into the lightly doped side: N_A x_p = N_D x_n.

pages.title: Junction capacitance
body: For an abrupt junction, W ∝ √(V_bi + V_R) and C_j = ε_s A/W.
For example, quadrupling the total depletion voltage doubles W and halves C_j.

pages.title: Diode law
body: I_D = I_S [exp(V/(n V_T)) − 1]. In strong forward bias, increasing V by about 60 mV gives 10× the current at room temperature if n = 1.
Small-signal resistance is r_d ≈ n V_T/I_D. At n = 1 and I_D = 10 mA, it is about 2.6 Ω.

pages.title: Reverse breakdown
body: Zener breakdown comes from tunneling through a narrow depletion layer. Avalanche comes from impact ionization.
Voltage is the area under the field profile. For a triangular profile, V ≈ E_max W/2.
Punch-through occurs when depletion spans a thin lightly doped region and reaches its far boundary.

pages.title: Stored charge and reverse recovery
body: Forward bias injects minority carriers. Q ≈ τ I_D, and the diffusion length is √(Dτ). This stored charge gives rise to diffusion capacitance.
When the diode switches to reverse bias, the reverse current clears stored charge. A larger removal current shortens storage time: t_s ≈ τ ln(1 + I_F/I_R).

required_questions.stem: At 300 K, an abrupt Si junction has NA = 4 × 10^16 cm⁻³, ND = 2 × 10^15 cm⁻³, and ni = 1 × 10^10 cm⁻³. Use VT = 0.0259 V. Find the equilibrium built-in voltage in volts.
required_questions.explain: Use Vbi = VT ln(NA ND / ni²). With these dopings, Vbi ≈ 0.710 V. Reverse bias changes the voltage across the depletion region, not this equilibrium built-in voltage.

required_questions.stem: At 300 K, an abrupt Si junction has NA = 3 × 10^16 cm⁻³, ND = 5 × 10^17 cm⁻³, and ni = 1 × 10^10 cm⁻³. Use VT = 0.0259 V. Find the equilibrium built-in voltage in volts.
required_questions.explain: Use Vbi = VT ln(NA ND / ni²). Substitution gives about 0.845 V.

required_questions.stem: An abrupt junction has W = 0.40 μm at zero bias and Vbi = 0.80 V. Its depletion width is proportional to the square root of the voltage across the depletion region. Find W at 2.40 V reverse bias.
required_questions.explain: The voltage across the depletion region grows from 0.80 V to 3.20 V. The width increases by √4 = 2, to 0.80 μm.

required_questions.stem: An abrupt junction has W = 0.30 μm at zero bias and Vbi = 0.70 V. Its depletion width is proportional to the square root of the voltage across the depletion region. Find W at 5.60 V reverse bias.
required_questions.explain: The depletion voltage rises from 0.70 V to 6.30 V. The width increases by √9 = 3, giving 0.90 μm.

required_questions.stem: A diode carries 0.20 mA in forward bias. Its forward voltage increases by 0.10 V at the same temperature. Use n = 2, VT = 0.025 V, and the exponential approximation to find the new current in mA.
required_questions.explain: The forward current is multiplied by exp(0.10 / (2 × 0.025)) = exp(2), giving 1.48 mA.

required_questions.stem: A diode carries 0.80 mA in forward bias. Its forward voltage increases by 0.075 V at the same temperature. Use n = 2, VT = 0.025 V, and the exponential approximation to find the new current in mA.
required_questions.explain: The current is multiplied by exp(0.075 / (2 × 0.025)) = exp(1.5), giving 3.59 mA.

required_questions.stem: An abrupt varactor has Cj = 15 pF at zero bias and Vbi = 0.75 V. Find Cj at 2.25 V reverse bias. Assume fixed area and uniform doping on each side.
required_questions.explain: The depletion voltage increases from 0.75 V to 3.00 V. The depletion width doubles, so its capacitance halves to 7.50 pF.

required_questions.stem: An abrupt varactor has Cj = 18 pF at zero bias and Vbi = 0.60 V. Find Cj at 4.80 V reverse bias. Assume fixed area and uniform doping on each side.
required_questions.explain: The depletion voltage grows from 0.60 V to 5.40 V. The depletion width triples, so Cj falls to 6.0 pF.

required_questions.stem: A diode carries 0.60 A just before switching. The driver removes stored charge with a constant 1.20 A reverse current. For lifetime 2.0 μs, use ts = τ ln(1 + IF / IR) to find the storage time in μs.
required_questions.explain: The ratio IF / IR is 0.5, so ts = 2.0 μs × ln(1.5) ≈ 0.811 μs. A larger reverse removal current shortens the storage time.

required_questions.stem: A diode carries 0.80 A just before switching. The driver removes stored charge with a constant 0.40 A reverse current. For lifetime 3.0 μs, use ts = τ ln(1 + IF / IR) to find the storage time in μs.
required_questions.explain: The ratio IF / IR is 2, so ts = 3.0 μs × ln(3) ≈ 3.30 μs.

required_questions.stem: An abrupt PN junction has N_A = 6 × 10^16 cm^-3, N_D = 2 × 10^16 cm^-3, and V_bi = 0.75 V. Its total depletion width at zero bias is 0.36 μm. At a reverse bias of 2.25 V, how far does depletion extend into the n side? Report the distance in μm.
required_questions.explain: The total junction voltage rises from 0.75 V to 3.00 V, so W doubles to 0.72 μm. From N_A x_p = N_D x_n and W = x_p + x_n, the n side takes 3/4 of W, giving 0.54 μm.

required_questions.stem: An abrupt PN junction has N_A = 2 × 10^16 cm^-3, N_D = 8 × 10^16 cm^-3, and V_bi = 0.65 V. Its total depletion width at zero bias is 0.40 μm. At a reverse bias of 1.95 V, how far does depletion extend into the p side? Report the distance in μm.
required_questions.explain: The junction voltage quadruples, so W doubles to 0.80 μm. The p side takes N_D/(N_A + N_D) = 4/5 of that width, giving 0.64 μm.

required_questions.stem: At 300 K, an abrupt silicon varactor has N_A = 5 × 10^16 cm^-3, N_D = 2 × 10^15 cm^-3, n_i = 1 × 10^10 cm^-3, and zero-bias capacitance 18 pF. Use V_T = 0.0259 V. Find the reverse bias needed to reduce the capacitance to 6 pF.
required_questions.explain: The doping values give V_bi ≈ 0.716 V. Reducing capacitance by a factor of 3 triples W and requires 9 times the total depletion voltage. Thus V_R = 8 V_bi ≈ 5.73 V.

required_questions.stem: At 300 K, an abrupt silicon varactor has N_A = 8 × 10^16 cm^-3, N_D = 5 × 10^15 cm^-3, n_i = 1 × 10^10 cm^-3, and zero-bias capacitance 20 pF. Use V_T = 0.0259 V. Find the reverse bias needed to reduce the capacitance to 10 pF.
required_questions.explain: The doping values give V_bi ≈ 0.752 V. Halving capacitance doubles W and requires 4 times the total depletion voltage. Thus V_R = 3 V_bi ≈ 2.25 V.

required_questions.stem: A forward-biased diode carries 0.50 mA. Its voltage increases by 0.052 V at constant temperature. Assume n = 2, V_T = 0.026 V, and the exponential approximation. Find the small-signal resistance at the new operating point.
required_questions.explain: The increase is n V_T, so current becomes 0.50 mA × exp(1) ≈ 1.36 mA. Use r_d = n V_T/I_D with current in amperes to get about 38.3 Ω.

required_questions.stem: A forward-biased diode carries 2.0 mA. Its voltage decreases by 0.026 V at constant temperature while it remains strongly forward biased. Assume n = 1, V_T = 0.026 V, and the exponential approximation. Find the small-signal resistance at the new operating point.
required_questions.explain: The voltage falls by n V_T, so current becomes 2.0 mA × exp(−1) ≈ 0.736 mA. The incremental resistance n V_T/I_D is about 35.3 Ω.

follow_up.stem: A reverse-biased varactor is in an LC resonator. The reverse voltage increases and L stays fixed. What happens to resonance frequency, and why?
choices: It rises because the depletion layer widens and the capacitance falls.
It falls because the depletion layer widens and the capacitance falls.
It rises because the depletion layer narrows and the capacitance rises.
It stays the same because the reverse DC current is small.
follow_up.explain: Wider depletion means smaller junction capacitance. The resonant frequency varies as 1/√(LC), so it rises.

follow_up.stem: The same PN diode switches from the same forward current in two tests. Driver B removes stored charge with twice the reverse current of driver A. Which test shows a shorter storage interval, and why?
choices: Driver A, because a smaller reverse current removes charge faster.
Driver B, because its stronger reverse current removes the stored carriers faster.
Both are equal because the initial forward current is the same.
Driver B takes longer because more reverse current creates more forward-stored charge.
follow_up.explain: At the same initial forward current, the stronger reverse removal current clears the stored minority carriers sooner.
